Elliott and others applied it to the wars of the 1790s in the Alpine and Italian river valleys, regions where Waldensian and other dissenters had been persecuted, so that the land "drank blood" for blood it had shed.
A literal, worldwide contamination of fresh water during the tribulation.
The angel of the waters: Righteous are You, O Holy One, who is and was

Jewish apocalyptic assigned angels to elements of creation: angels of the winds, clouds, snow and waters (Jubilees 2:2; 1 Enoch 60:11-22; 66:1-2; compare Revelation 7:1; 14:18). Confessing God's justice when judgment falls is a known form (a "doxology of judgment"): Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 119:137; Prayer of Azariah (Daniel 3:27 in the Greek); Tobit 3:2.
Even the angel responsible for the waters agrees that their ruin is just. God is called the One "who is and who was" without "who is to come" (as in 11:17), because in these judgments he has come.
They spilled the blood of saints and prophets, and You gave them blood to drink

Isaiah 49:26 says the oppressors will be drunk with their own blood. Wisdom of Solomon 11:6-7 interprets the Nile plague as a fitting punishment for Pharaoh's decree to drown Hebrew infants, and states the principle that one is punished by the means of one's sin (11:16). Jesus charged Jerusalem with the blood of the prophets and said it would come on "this generation" (Matthew 23:29-36; Luke 11:47-51).
Roman executions of Christians under Nero (Tacitus, Annals 15.44) were recent memory if Revelation was written either in the 60s or the 90s.

Strict justice (lex talionis): punishment fits the crime. The killers of God's witnesses are made to "drink" blood. "As they deserve" (Greek axioi eisin) is a stark contrast with the Lamb, who is "worthy" (axios) in 5:9.
Applies to Jerusalem, which Jesus said had killed the prophets and on which all the righteous blood would come within that generation (Matthew 23:35-36; Luke 13:33).
Refers to the persecutors of tribulation saints in the end-time, who receive just retribution.
A permanent principle: persecuting powers in every age reap what they sow.
The altar replies: Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments

The souls of the martyrs cried out from under the altar for vindication (Revelation 6:9-10); the prayers of the saints rose from the golden altar and fire from it was thrown to the earth (8:3-5); a voice came from the altar's horns (9:13). Blood poured at the altar's base (Leviticus 4:7) gives the image its force.

The altar, standing for the martyrs and the prayers of the saints, confirms that the long cry "How long?" has been answered justly. The double witness (angel and altar) follows the legal rule of two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15).
The sun given power to scorch people with fire

Deuteronomy 32:24 threatens "burning heat"; Malachi 4:1 speaks of a day burning like an oven. It reverses the promise to the redeemed that the sun will not strike them (Isaiah 49:10; Revelation 7:16). The fourth trumpet darkened a third of the sun (8:12).
In the hot climate of Asia and Judea, heat and drought meant crop failure and death; sun worship (Sol Invictus later, Helios and Apollo in the first century) was widespread.
Creation itself turns against those who worship the creature. The fourth bowl reverses the protection promised to the sealed people of God.
Barnes and Elliott applied it to the devastating wars of Napoleon, which "scorched" Europe, especially the papal and Catholic powers.
A literal intensification of solar heat in the last days.
Judgment through the natural order, which in every age can become a scourge on rebellious people.
They cursed the name of God and did not repent and give Him glory

Pharaoh hardened his heart after each plague (Exodus 8:15, 32; 9:34-35). Amos 4:6-11 repeats after each disaster "yet you did not return to me". Contrast Revelation 11:13, where survivors give glory to God, and 15:4, where nations fear and glorify him.
Cursing gods in misfortune was known in antiquity; blasphemy here echoes the beast's own blasphemies (13:5-6).
The plagues are not only punitive but also a call to repent, yet hardened people refuse. The repeated refrain shows that suffering alone does not change hearts, and justifies the final judgment.
A picture of the hardening that sets in whenever people persist in idolatry; judgment exposes rather than changes the heart.
Describes the attitude of the unbelieving world in the final days of the tribulation.
Bowl on the throne of the beast: its kingdom plunged into darkness

The ninth Egyptian plague brought a darkness that could be felt (Exodus 10:21-23); Wisdom of Solomon 17 elaborates it as a darkness of terror and guilt. The prophets speak of darkness on the day of the LORD (Joel 2:2; Amos 5:18-20; Isaiah 60:2). The dragon gave the beast his throne (Revelation 13:2).
The "throne" points to the seat of imperial power. The Roman world experienced the near-collapse of the empire in the civil wars of AD 68-69 (the year of four emperors), after Nero's suicide.
God strikes the centre of the beast's power. Darkness signals confusion, collapse of authority and despair.
Rome's chaos in AD 68-69, when Nero died and rival emperors fought, so that the beast's kingdom was plunged into darkness (Gentry; Chilton relates it more to Jerusalem's distress).
The humiliation of the papal see (the beast's throne) when French armies occupied Rome and took Pope Pius VI captive (1798), followed by the Napoleonic suppression of papal power.
Supernatural darkness over the Antichrist's capital and empire near the end of the tribulation (Walvoord).
Every godless regime eventually experiences the breakdown of its power, a foretaste of final judgment.
Men gnawed their tongues in anguish
Compare "weeping and gnashing of teeth" in the teaching of Jesus (Matthew 8:12; 13:42) and the anguish in darkness of Wisdom of Solomon 17.
A vivid image of agony and helpless rage. Together with "pains and sores" it shows that the bowls accumulate rather than replace one another.
The great river Euphrates dried up

The Euphrates was the northern boundary of the promised land (Genesis 15:18) and the river of Babylon and Assyria, from beyond which invaders came (Isaiah 8:7; Jeremiah 46:10). God dried waters for his people at the Red Sea (Exodus 14) and the Jordan (Joshua 3), and promised to dry the river again (Isaiah 11:15-16; 44:27; Jeremiah 50:38; 51:36). Cyrus took Babylon by diverting the Euphrates (Herodotus 1.191; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 7.5). The sixth trumpet released angels bound at the Euphrates (Revelation 9:14).

For Rome the Euphrates was the frontier with Parthia, the one power Rome feared. The Nero redivivus legend imagined Nero returning from beyond the Euphrates with Parthian armies to destroy Rome (Sibylline Oracles 4.119-139; 5.137-154).
A barrier that held back invading armies is removed by God himself. The Cyrus story shows Babylon's fall coming through the drying of its river, so the image prepares for Babylon's judgment in 16:19.

Gentry and Chilton note that Titus' army included troops drawn from the Euphrates frontier and from eastern client kings (Josephus, Jewish War 5.40-46; Tacitus, Histories 5.1): the way was opened for armies to come against Jerusalem.
The drying up of the Ottoman (Turkish) empire that ruled the Euphrates region, a decline that historicists from the 1820s onward identified and watched (Elliott, Barnes).
A literal drying of the Euphrates (perhaps aided by dams) that lets eastern armies march toward Israel for Armageddon (Walvoord).
God removes the restraints on evil so that the forces of the world gather for their final defeat; Babylon falls as it did to Cyrus.
The kings of the East

Literally "the kings from the rising of the sun". Cyrus is the one "from the east" whom God calls against Babylon (Isaiah 41:2, 25; 46:11). In Revelation 7:2 the sealing angel comes from the rising of the sun.
Parthian rulers styled themselves "king of kings" and were the classic eastern threat; their invasion was a stock fear of the Roman East.

Eastern rulers coming to make war. Most read them as hostile forces drawn into the final battle; a minority reading (some idealists, following the Cyrus typology) sees them as instruments of God against Babylon, or even as Christ and his people.
Roman generals and eastern client kings (Agrippa II, Antiochus of Commagene, Sohaemus of Emesa, Malchus of Arabia) who joined Vespasian and Titus against Jerusalem.
Variously the converted Jews or Eastern peoples whose way is opened by the decline of Islam, in preparation for Christ's kingdom.
A literal coalition of Asian nations, often connected with the 200 million of Revelation 9:16 (Walvoord).
Nations hostile to God whom he allows to gather; in the Cyrus pattern they also become agents of Babylon's downfall.
Three unclean spirits like frogs from the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet

The second Egyptian plague filled the land with frogs (Exodus 8:1-15; Psalm 78:45; 105:30). Frogs were unclean animals (Leviticus 11:9-12, 41-42). Lying spirits that entice kings to battle recall 1 Kings 22:19-23, where a deceiving spirit lures Ahab to his death.
In Zoroastrian (Persian) belief, frogs were among the noxious creatures of the evil spirit. Ancient writers mocked the croaking of frogs as empty noise.

Three spirits from three mouths form an unholy trinity of propaganda. They come from mouths because their power is deceptive speech that gathers the kings. They are demonic, working signs (compare 13:13-14).
The lying propaganda that drew the Jewish rebels and the nations into the war of AD 66-70, including false prophets who promised deliverance (Josephus, Jewish War 6.285-288).

Nineteenth-century historicists identified three spreading influences of their day; Elliott linked them to infidelity, popery and a priestly sacramentalism, while others named paganism, papalism and Islam.
Literal demonic emissaries who perform miracles to draw world leaders to Armageddon.
The ideologies, lies and propaganda by which evil powers in every age mobilise the world against God and his people.
The false prophet

Named here for the first time, the false prophet is the beast from the land (Revelation 13:11-17; see 19:20; 20:10). Deuteronomy 13:1-5 warns against prophets who work signs to lead Israel to other gods; Jesus warned of false prophets performing signs (Matthew 24:11, 24).
The land beast resembles the provincial priesthood of the imperial cult in Asia, the councils and high priests who organised emperor worship and could use statues that seemed to speak or move.
The religious power that serves the political beast by deception, persuading people to worship it.
Some (Chilton) see the apostate Jewish religious leadership that allied with Rome; others the provincial imperial cult.
The papal hierarchy and clergy as the spiritual arm of the papal system.
A future individual religious leader who promotes the worship of the Antichrist.
False religion and ideology that legitimise oppressive power in every era.
Battle on the great day of God the Almighty

The day of the LORD is "great" in Joel 2:11, 31 and Zephaniah 1:14. The prophets foresee God gathering the nations for judgment: Joel 3:2, 9-14 (the valley of Jehoshaphat), Zephaniah 3:8, Zechariah 12:3 and 14:2 (all nations against Jerusalem), and Ezekiel 38-39 (Gog). The same gathering reappears in Revelation 19:19 and 20:8, and Psalm 2:2 shows the kings gathered against the LORD and his Anointed.

The demonic spirits think they are gathering the kings for their own war, but in fact they bring them to God's day of judgment. Many scholars note that the definite article ("the battle") and the repeated wording connect 16:14, 19:19 and 20:8 as one final battle.
The battles of 16:14, 19:19 and 20:8 are the same final conflict described three times; this supports reading Revelation 20 as recapitulating the church age (Beale, Riddlebarger).
The campaign of Armageddon at the end of the tribulation, ended by Christ's return in 19:11-21; the battle of 20:8 is a separate revolt after the millennium.
The "day" of the Lord's judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, when Rome and its allies gathered against the city.
Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who stays awake and clothed

Jesus used the image of the thief for his coming (Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39), and Paul and Peter echo it (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). Sardis is warned that Christ will come like a thief (Revelation 3:3) and Laodicea told to buy white garments to cover its nakedness (3:18). The Mishnah (compiled c. 200, later than Revelation) describes the captain of the Temple Mount making night rounds; a Levite found asleep at his post could be beaten and have his clothes burned (Mishnah Middot 1:2).
Nakedness and public exposure were deep shame in honour-shame cultures; prisoners and the defeated were stripped.

A sudden interruption in the narrative, in Christ's own voice, and the third of Revelation's seven beatitudes. In the middle of the gathering for battle, readers are told to stay alert and keep their garments: faithful lives. It shows that the vision is aimed at the church's present conduct.
Christ's coming in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, which Jesus said would come within that generation; Christians were to be ready to flee (Luke 21:20-22).
The Parousia itself, which occurred in AD 70.
The Second Coming at the end of the tribulation; dispensationalists apply the warning to tribulation believers rather than to a church already raptured.
The one Second Coming at the end of the age, for which the church must always be ready.
The place called in Hebrew Armageddon

Most take Har-Magedon as Hebrew "mountain of Megiddo". Megiddo guarded the pass into the Jezreel valley and was a famous battlefield: Deborah and Barak defeated the kings of Canaan "by the waters of Megiddo" (Judges 5:19); King Josiah fell there (2 Kings 23:29-30; 2 Chronicles 35:22); Zechariah 12:11 speaks of great mourning "in the plain of Megiddo" over one whom they pierced (compare Revelation 1:7). But Megiddo is a mound, not a mountain, and there was no known "mount of Megiddo". Alternatives include "mount of assembly" (har mo'ed, the mountain of the gods in Isaiah 14:13), nearby Mount Carmel (where Elijah defeated the prophets of Baal, 1 Kings 18), or Mount Zion/Jerusalem, where the prophets place the final battle (Joel 3; Zechariah 12; 14; Ezekiel 38-39 on "the mountains of Israel").
The Jezreel valley below Megiddo was a corridor for armies from Thutmose III (15th century BC) onward; "in Hebrew" signals a riddle-like name, as with Abaddon (9:11).

The name evokes the place where God's enemies are defeated and the world mourns. Whether it is a literal location or a symbolic name for the final battle is disputed; most scholars think John chose a name with rich associations rather than a map reference.
A literal staging area in the valley of Jezreel near Megiddo for a campaign that culminates at Jerusalem when Christ returns (Walvoord; Thomas).
A symbolic name recalling Israel's great defeats and mourning, applied to the armies gathered against Jerusalem in AD 66-70 (Chilton).
The final great conflict between Christ and the coalition of papal, infidel and anti-Christian powers, often linked by its interpreters with events and alliances of their own day.
Not a geographical place but a symbol of the final battle in which the world gathers against the church and is destroyed by Christ; the same event as 19:19-21 and 20:7-10.
Beale and others read it as a symbolic "Megiddo-mountain" that blends Megiddo with the mountains of Israel of Ezekiel 38-39, describing the last attack on God's people.
The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air

Satan is called "the ruler of the power of the air" in Ephesians 2:2; Jewish cosmology placed evil spirits in the lower heavens (2 Enoch; Testament of Benjamin 3:4). The air is also the source of the storm that follows (lightning, thunder, hail).
Greek physics counted air as one of the four elements; after earth, sea, waters and sun, the air completes the elements struck.
The last bowl reaches the whole environment of human life and, for many interpreters, the realm of the demonic powers. It produces the final storm and earthquake.
A loud voice from the throne: It is done!

The Greek gegonen recalls Ezekiel 39:8 ("it is coming and it shall be done") about the defeat of Gog. It anticipates Revelation 21:6 ("It is done") at the new creation, and resembles Jesus' cry "It is finished" (John 19:30), though the verb differs.
God's judgment on evil is complete. The voice from the throne in the temple shows it is God's own declaration.
The end of the old covenant order with the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.
The completion of God's wrath at the very end of the tribulation, just before Christ returns.
The final judgment that ends history, seen from the perspective of the seventh and last bowl.
A great earthquake such as had never occurred since men were on the earth

Lightning, rumblings and thunder recall God's appearance at Sinai (Exodus 19:16-19) and grow in intensity through Revelation (4:5; 8:5; 11:19; 16:18). The prophets foresee God shaking heaven and earth (Haggai 2:6; Hebrews 12:26-27) and a great earthquake in the land in the battle with Gog (Ezekiel 38:19-20; Zechariah 14:4-5). "Such as had never been" echoes Daniel 12:1 and Exodus 9:18, 24.

Asia Minor was prone to earthquakes. Tacitus records the AD 17 earthquake that destroyed twelve cities in one night, including Sardis and Philadelphia (Annals 2.47), and Laodicea was destroyed in AD 60.

The climax of God's appearing in judgment: the whole structure of human society is shaken. Many see the language of cosmic shaking as covenantal imagery for the end of an order (as in Haggai 2:6); others as literal and final.
Covenantal "decreation" language for the end of the Jewish order in AD 70, interpreted through Hebrews 12:26-28, where the shaking removes the old so the unshakable kingdom remains.
A literal, unprecedented global earthquake at the end of the tribulation (Zechariah 14:4).
The final shaking of creation at the last judgment.
The great city split into three parts; the cities of the nations collapsed

In Ezekiel 5:1-12 the prophet divides his shaved hair into three parts as a sign of Jerusalem's fate: a third burned in the city, a third struck by the sword, a third scattered. Zechariah 14:4 sees the Mount of Olives split by an earthquake. "The great city" is Jerusalem in Revelation 11:8 ("where their Lord was crucified") and Babylon in 14:8, 17:18 and 18:10-21.
Josephus describes Jerusalem during the siege as split into three warring factions under John of Gischala, Simon bar Giora and Eleazar (Jewish War 5.1-4). Rome in AD 69 was torn by civil war.
The great city is utterly broken, and with it the cities of the nations that shared its life. The identity of "the great city" is central to the debate about Babylon.
The great city is Jerusalem (as in 11:8), divided into three factions during the siege and destroyed in AD 70; the Ezekiel 5 pattern confirms it (Chilton, Gentry).
Papal Rome and the political-religious system it headed, broken up in the final judgment; the "cities of the nations" are the kingdoms of Christendom.
Either a literal end-time Babylon or Jerusalem split by a literal earthquake (Zechariah 14:4); Walvoord takes the great city as Babylon, distinct from the cities of the nations.
The great city is the world city of every age, human society organised against God, which collapses at the end.
God remembered Babylon the great and gave her the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath

The cup of God's wrath is a stock prophetic image: Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17, 22 (Jerusalem drinks it); Jeremiah 25:15-29 (the nations, Babylon last); Jeremiah 51:7 (Babylon a golden cup in the LORD's hand). The Qumran Habakkuk commentary says the Wicked Priest will drink the cup of the LORD's wrath (1QpHab 11:10-15). "God remembered" is covenant language (Genesis 8:1; Exodus 2:24) here used for judgment (Psalm 137:7).
Wine was mixed with water in Greek and Roman custom; "unmixed" wine (14:10) was strong and intoxicating. Babylon's own cup of seduction (17:4; 18:6) is turned back on her.
God has not forgotten the city's crimes; she must drink the full cup she made others drink. The verse previews chapters 17-18, which expand the fall of Babylon.
Every island fled and no mountain could be found
Compare the sixth seal (Revelation 6:14) and the great white throne (20:11). Mountains melt and flee at God's coming (Judges 5:5; Psalm 97:5; Nahum 1:5; Isaiah 40:4; 1 Enoch 1:6).

The stable features of creation give way before God's presence. Interpreters differ whether this is literal geological upheaval or the prophetic language of theophany used for the fall of world orders.
Prophetic theophany imagery (as in Isaiah 13 for Babylon or Isaiah 34 for Edom) for the collapse of a nation, here Israel and its world in AD 70.
Literal topographical changes at Christ's return.
The dissolution of the present order at the final judgment (20:11).
Great hailstones weighing about a hundred pounds

The seventh Egyptian plague was hail with fire (Exodus 9:22-26); God threw hailstones on the Amorites (Joshua 10:11) and will rain hail on Gog (Ezekiel 38:22); hail is in God's storehouse for the day of battle (Job 38:22-23; Isaiah 28:2, 17). The penalty for blasphemy in the law was stoning (Leviticus 24:16), and here those who blaspheme are stoned from heaven.

The Greek talantiaia means "the weight of a talent", roughly 20 to 45 kg depending on the standard. Josephus says the Roman siege engines at Jerusalem threw white stones weighing a talent, and that watchmen shouted a warning as each one came (Jewish War 5.269-273).
The final, crushing blow of judgment from heaven, yet the survivors still curse God.
Chilton and others point to Josephus' talent-weight stones hurled by Roman catapults into Jerusalem in AD 70: the covenant penalty of stoning for blasphemy inflicted on the city.
Literal, enormous hail falling at the end of the tribulation.
A symbol of overwhelming final judgment, modelled on the Egyptian plague of hail.

The bowls are the covenant judgments on Jerusalem and the land culminating in AD 70. Sores recall the Deuteronomy 28 curses; the sea and rivers of blood recall the massacres Josephus describes; the Euphrates opens for Rome's eastern legions and client kings; Armageddon symbolises the gathering of armies against Jerusalem; the great city split in three is Jerusalem divided into factions and destroyed; the talent-weight hail matches the Roman catapult stones (Chilton, Gentry). Some preterists who identify Babylon with Rome read the fifth bowl as Rome's civil war of AD 68-69.

Agrees with the partial preterist mapping onto AD 66-70 but holds that "It is done" marks the full end of redemptive history, the Parousia and the judgment of the dead, all fulfilled in AD 70 (King, Preston). Critics, including partial preterists, say this collapses the final resurrection and Second Coming into a past event in a way the historic creeds deny; proponents answer that the New Testament time statements require it.

The bowls fall from the French Revolution onward: the ulcer of revolutionary infidelity (first), the naval wars (second), the river campaigns in persecuting lands (third), the Napoleonic wars (fourth), the humbling of the papal throne in 1798-1809 (fifth), the drying of Ottoman power (sixth), and a still-future final judgment (seventh) (Elliott, Barnes).

The bowls are literal, worldwide plagues in the last part of the future tribulation. The Euphrates will be dried for eastern armies; demonic spirits will gather the nations to the valley of Megiddo; Christ will return to defeat them; a literal earthquake will split Jerusalem or end-time Babylon and level the cities of the world (Walvoord, Thomas). Dispensationalists see the church already raptured; historic premillennialists (Ladd) see the church present and protected through these judgments.

The bowls portray God's judgments on the impenitent in every age, culminating in the last judgment. Armageddon is not a place on a map but the final attack of the world on the church, the same battle as 19:19 and 20:8. The constant refrain "they did not repent" exposes the hardening of human hearts (Hendriksen, Milligan).

Beale reads the bowls as covering the period between Christ's first and second comings while culminating in the end, with Armageddon as a symbolic name for the final battle that recapitulates 19:19-21 and 20:7-10. Osborne leans futurist while stressing the symbolic use of Exodus imagery.
The repeated description of a single final battle (16:14; 19:19; 20:8) supports reading Revelation 20 as a recapitulation of the church age rather than a sequel to chapter 19.

Armageddon is the climactic campaign of the seven-year tribulation, after which Christ sets up a literal thousand-year reign in Jerusalem; the Gog and Magog revolt of 20:8 is a separate event after the millennium.
Why do the bowls follow the order of the trumpets (earth, sea, rivers, sun) while being total rather than partial? What does this suggest about the structure of Revelation?
The angel of the waters and the altar both declare God's judgments just. How does the "blood for blood" principle (16:6) fit with the Lamb who conquers by his own blood?
Is Armageddon a place, a symbol or both? What do the associations of Megiddo (Judges 5, 2 Kings 23, Zechariah 12) add to the image?
Why does Christ's beatitude about watchfulness (16:15) interrupt the gathering for battle?
Who is "the great city" of 16:19: Jerusalem (11:8), Rome, a future city or the world system? What clues in the text point each way?
The Great Prostitute on the Scarlet Beast
The fall of Babylon (Revelation 17:1-19:10)

One of the bowl angels shows John the judgment of the great prostitute who sits on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed immorality. In a wilderness he sees a woman dressed in purple and scarlet, glittering with gold and pearls, holding a golden cup of abominations and riding a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns. Her forehead bears the name "Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes", and she is drunk with the blood of the saints. The angel explains the mystery: the beast "was, and is not, and is about to come up from the abyss"; its seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings, five fallen, one present and one still to come, and the beast itself is an eighth; its ten horns are ten kings who rule with it for one hour and make war on the Lamb, who conquers them. Finally the beast and the ten horns turn on the prostitute, strip her, devour her flesh and burn her, because God put it into their hearts; the woman is "the great city that rules over the kings of the earth".
Invitation: the judgment of the great prostitute
The vision: the woman on the scarlet beast, her dress, cup, name and drunkenness
The mystery of the beast that was, is not and will come
Seven heads: seven mountains and seven kings; the eighth
Ten horns: ten kings who war against the Lamb and lose
The waters explained; the beast destroys the prostitute; the woman is the great city

The chapter is a portrait of a city as a prostitute, a standard prophetic image. Isaiah calls Jerusalem a harlot (Isaiah 1:21); Jeremiah 2-3 and Ezekiel 16 and 23 develop at length the picture of Jerusalem and Samaria as adulterous women; Hosea applies it to Israel. But pagan cities are also harlots: Tyre is a forgotten prostitute singing for her trade (Isaiah 23:15-18) and Nineveh is the "mistress of sorceries" who seduced nations (Nahum 3:4). Babylon itself is the city that "dwells on many waters" (Jeremiah 51:13), a golden cup in the LORD's hand that made the nations drunk (Jeremiah 51:7), a queen who says she will never be a widow (Isaiah 47:7-8). After AD 70, Jewish writings used "Babylon" as a code name for Rome, which like Nebuchadnezzar had destroyed the temple (4 Ezra 3:1-2, 28-31; 2 Baruch 10:1-3; 11:1; 67:7; Sibylline Oracles 5.143, 159), and 1 Peter 5:13 uses Babylon for the city where Peter writes, usually taken as Rome. The beast and its heads and horns come from Daniel 7, where the fourth beast has ten horns and a little horn that blasphemes and wars against the saints.

The Roman setting is vivid. Rome was famous as the city on seven hills (Virgil, Georgics 2.535; Horace, Carmen Saeculare 7; Martial 4.64; Cicero, Letters to Atticus 6.5), celebrated annually in the Septimontium festival. A sestertius of Vespasian (AD 71) shows the goddess Roma seated on the seven hills with the river Tiber at her feet, a remarkable parallel to a woman seated on seven mountains by many waters. The goddess Roma was worshipped in temples across Asia Minor, often alongside the emperor. The "was, is not, will come" riddle evokes the Nero redivivus legend, the rumour that Nero had not truly died (or would rise) and would return from the east (Tacitus, Histories 2.8-9; Suetonius, Nero 57; Dio Cassius 64.9). The identity of Babylon is one of the great disputes of Revelation study: first-century Rome; first-century Jerusalem; papal Rome; a future rebuilt Babylon or end-time world capital; or the world system in every age. The arguments are summarised in the readings below, and each view is held by careful scholars.
The great prostitute

In the prophets a city that forsakes God or trades with the nations for gain is a prostitute: Jerusalem (Isaiah 1:21; Jeremiah 3:1-10; Ezekiel 16; 23), Samaria (Ezekiel 23), Israel (Hosea 2), Tyre (Isaiah 23:15-18) and Nineveh (Nahum 3:4). The image stands in deliberate contrast to the Bride, the New Jerusalem, introduced with the same formula ("one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said, Come, I will show you", 17:1; 21:9).

Prostitution was legal and widespread in Roman cities; brothels and courtesans were part of urban life. "Fornication" was also a familiar metaphor for idolatry and for commercial and political compromise.

The prostitute is a city whose power over the nations rests on seduction: idolatry, economic exploitation and political alliance. The parallel with the Bride invites a "tale of two cities", the city of man and the city of God.
